correctness.rationale: A blade vertex has degree m. If its blade contains the center color, the center-colored block must have at least ceil(m/2) blade vertices, while any other color block must have at least ceil(m/2)+1 vertices; these bounds rule out a mixed blade. If the center color is absent, two non-center blocks cannot both fit, so the blade is again monochromatic. The center condition then becomes exactly b>=ceil(n/2) for the number b of center-colored blades. The Stirling formula counts choices of non-center blades and onto assignments to the remaining labeled colors. Exhaustive direct checks and exact counts agree in the tested range.

originality.rationale: The initiating paper explicitly states the friendship-graph scalar value, so that m=2 numerical case is treated as prior coverage. Its inspected full text does not state a theorem for generalized windmills K_1 join nK_m, nor a classification of all colorings, a full color-count spectrum, or an exact coloring count. published-finding corpus searches using majority-C, generalized-windmill, join-of-cliques, friendship, spectrum, and Stirling/enumeration formulations found no covering result. The final claim strictly contains the credited friendship scalar special case and adds independent structural and enumerative information.
residual_risks: The scalar m=2 friendship value is explicitly prior and is not claimed as novel by itself.
Generalized windmills can be indexed under clique bouquets or windmill variants, so a poorly indexed equivalent family theorem could escape keyword search.
Majority C-coloring is a new and active invariant, so concurrent follow-up work may not yet be indexed.

value.rationale: Generalized windmills form a canonical clique-bouquet extension of the friendship family already singled out by the initiating paper. The result gives a complete structural classification for every blade size, reveals that the maximum is unexpectedly independent of blade order once m>=2, determines every feasible color count, and counts all surjective colorings exactly by a Stirling transform. This is substantially more information than the already known friendship scalar value.
